segments.voice: Yesterday in the Devi Mahatmya, every god gave the goddess something of his own, the mountain gave her a lion, and her breaths became armies. What did you give away that was really yours? Day one thousand sixty-five.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `EACH GOD GIVES FROM HIS OWN.`

segments.voice: The generals are dead. Their armies are scattered. And now the buffalo himself comes onto the field. In the third chapter, Mahisha arrives in his own form, a huge buffalo, and the text makes him frightening: he tramples the goddess's troops with his hooves, flings them with his horns, lashes them with his tail. His hooves crack the ground. His breath tosses mountains through the air. He charges at her lion. And the goddess, the text says, grows angry. This is the fight the whole second story has been building to, and it's a scene shown in images of her: a goddess, a lion, and a buffalo at her feet. Today, how the text actually tells it.
screen: `THE BUFFALO HIMSELF.` → `HE CHARGES THE LION.` → `THE SCENE THE IMAGES FREEZE.`

segments.voice: She throws her noose around him, and he stops being a buffalo. He becomes a lion. She cuts off its head, and there's a man with a sword in its place. She shoots him down with arrows, and he becomes a great elephant, dragging her lion with his trunk. She cuts off the trunk. And he's a buffalo again, shaking the worlds. A shape-shifter. Every time she has him, he becomes something else. And then the text does something you might not expect in a battle. The goddess stops, and drinks. She drinks from her cup again and again, and she laughs, her eyes going red. Mahisha, full of his own strength, bellows and hurls mountains at her with his horns. And she speaks to him. In paraphrase: roar, roar for a moment, you fool, while I drink. When I've killed you, the gods will soon be roaring here instead. Then she leaps. She sets her foot on his neck and pierces him with her spear. Pinned under her foot, he starts to come out of the buffalo's mouth in his real form, only halfway out, still fighting. And she cuts off his head with her great sword. The gods rejoice. Look at the shape of it. Mahisha's power is changing form. He never stays one thing long enough to be held. She meets each shape as it comes. Then, in the middle of it all, she stops. She drinks, she laughs, and she lets him roar. She isn't hurried by him. When she moves again, she moves once, and he's pinned and has to show himself. The story ends with a buffalo half out of its own skin, and the goddess standing on its neck.
screen: `A BUFFALO, A LION, A MAN, AN ELEPHANT.` · `SHE STOPS, DRINKS, AND LAUGHS.` · `ROAR FOR A MOMENT, YOU FOOL.` · `HALF OUT OF HIS OWN SKIN.` · then, large: `SHE WAITS UNTIL HE SHOWS HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a pause in the middle of the fight. Settle where you are, with whatever today still holds undone. Don't solve any of it. Let the noise of it keep going, like a roar in the distance, and let the breath be unhurried anyway. Breathe in slowly, as if taking a long drink. Breathe out slowly. Let the next thing wait a few breaths. If you pray, you can rest in the goddess, or in God, by the names you already use. If you don't, let the breath be the place you stand. The bell holds the time.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, the end of its second story: Mahisha the shape-shifter, pinned under the goddess's foot until he has to show himself.
Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. Today, in the middle of a busy stretch, stop for one slow drink of water, unhurried, before you go back in. Day one thousand sixty-five.

howItsDone: The goddess slaying Mahisha, Mahishasuramardini, is a familiar image of Durga, and during Durga Puja and Navaratri Hindus worship images that show her with her foot on the buffalo and Mahisha emerging from it.

fork.setup: you're the goddess. Mahisha keeps changing shape: lion, man, elephant, buffalo. he's hurling mountains at you. what do you do?
options: chase every new shape as fast as you can.
stop, drink, laugh, and then pin him under your foot.
fork.reveal: she drinks and laughs, tells him to roar for a moment, then leaps, sets her foot on his neck, and beheads him as he comes half out of the buffalo.

original.note: Sanskrit: mahiṣāsura-mardinī, she who crushes the buffalo demon. A name for the goddess.

trapdoor: what you thought: a goddess kills a buffalo.
what it means: Mahisha keeps changing shape; she meets each one, pauses unhurried, and strikes once he is pinned and has to come out in his own form.
what a scholar hears: chapter 3, where the goddess drinks before the kill and he emerges half out of the buffalo's mouth: the moment Mahishasuramardini images show.
recall: a saying: Akka Mahadevi's short free poems

notes: Chapter 3 paraphrased: Mahisha as buffalo tramples the troops; the noose; lion, man with sword, elephant dragging the lion, buffalo again; the goddess drinks (the divine drink/madhu) again and again and laughs with reddened eyes; her words (garja garja kṣaṇaṃ mūḍha madhu yāvat pibāmy aham...) paraphrased as 'roar for a moment, you fool, while I drink; when I've killed you the gods will soon roar here'; foot on his neck, spear, he emerges half from the buffalo's mouth, beheaded with the great sword. Confirm.
The drink is rendered 'from her cup' (Kubera's gift on 1064). Some traditions read the madhu as wine, others as honey or nectar; the script avoids naming it. Confirm.
'Some readers hear it about a restless mind' is an interpretive reading, attributed and not ranked. Confirm it is acceptable to a Keeper.
The hook says 'a scene her images often freeze' rather than any superlative; confirm.

Editor pass: 'his roar splits the ground' became 'his hooves crack the ground' (the text has the earth broken by his hooves); 'her images often freeze' softened; the teach claimed she doesn't chase his shapes, but she answers each one, so it now says she meets each shape and then pauses unhurried; the restless-mind reading and the mind-watching practice and carry were cut because 1069 makes the same move with Raktabija; the new practice and carry are a pause mid-fight, taken from her stopping to drink.
